disease_info: Persistent Depressive Disorder (dysthymia) is a chronic mood disorder characterized by a persistently low or dysphoric mood lasting at least two years in adults, with no symptom-free periods longer than two months. It often presents with less dramatic but more enduring impairment than major depressive disorder, involving low mood plus associated features such as low energy, poor concentration, low self-esteem, appetite or sleep changes, or hopelessness. The course is typically insidious and long-standing, frequently beginning after stressful life events or in the context of personality and environmental vulnerabilities, and can coexist with superimposed major depressive episodes ("double depression"). It is distinguished from normal sadness or adjustment reactions by its duration, pervasiveness across life domains, and associated functional impairment, and from major depressive disorder by its chronic, more subtle, and trait-like presentation.

narrative.stressor: Around two and a half years ago, Larissa’s bank merged with a larger institution, leading to new productivity metrics, stricter sales targets, and the loss of several longtime colleagues she had mentored. The shift from collaborative counseling to a more transactional, quota-driven environment gradually eroded the sense of purpose she had long drawn from helping clients stabilize their finances, and she began cutting back on her workshops and community art‑based education sessions as work demands spilled into evenings and weekends. Over the following two years, she found herself repeatedly turning down hiking outings, skipping pottery classes, and letting her garden go untended, telling friends she was "too tired" and struggling to keep up with the organizational tasks she once relished. She finally agreed to see her primary care doctor—who referred her for psychiatric evaluation—after she noticed that even a planned art‑and‑foliage road trip to the Shenandoah Valley felt like an obligation rather than something to look forward to, and her performance reviews began to mention decreased initiative and engagement.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like the future has just kind of closed in on me, like there isn’t much to look forward to anymore.”

narrative.stressor: John’s low mood began shortly after he graduated high school and started working full‑time as a medical assistant instead of following his friends to college, a decision driven by finances and family expectations. What he assumed would be a temporary, practical step became an ongoing routine of early shifts at the rural clinic, evening DIY projects, and solitary gaming, and over the next two years he increasingly compared himself to peers posting about campus life and internships, questioning whether he had already limited his future. As he juggled work, night classes toward an associate degree, and volunteer health fairs, he noticed himself falling behind on coursework, abandoning guitar practice, and avoiding basketball games because he felt mentally "checked out" and unable to make decisions about his next steps. He finally accepted a referral from a nurse practitioner at the clinic—who noticed his growing indecisiveness about even simple tasks and his stalled plans for further training—after he admitted he’d been feeling this way for "a couple of years" and couldn’t seem to get his focus or drive back.
narrative.chief_complaint: “For the last couple of years I just can’t think clearly or make up my mind about anything, even simple stuff.”

narrative.stressor: Ashley traces the beginning of her prolonged downturn to when she and her spouse relocated from Southern California to the Bay Area for her promotion to senior physical scientist just over two years ago, a move that disrupted her familiar routines and social supports. The new role intensified her perfectionistic tendencies, and at the same time her spouse struggled to find comparable work, leading to simmering tension at home and fewer shared activities like hiking or piano recitals that once anchored their relationship. Over the next two years, Ashley increasingly stayed late at the lab to avoid difficult conversations, gradually withdrew from neighborhood plant‑swap gatherings, and found that even her normally soothing hobbies—precision baking, stargazing, detailed travel planning—felt like obligations rather than pleasures, contributing to growing strain in the marriage. After a particularly tense argument in which her spouse pointed out that she seemed emotionally absent and "unreachable" for more than a year, Ashley agreed to see a psychiatrist at the suggestion of her primary care physician, concerned that her ongoing state was starting to jeopardize both her relationship and her ability to lead her research team effectively.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve felt low and weighed down almost all the time for the last couple of years, and it just never really lifts.”
